planting.note: Sow in fall so winter cold moist-stratifies the seed naturally, into average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun; heath aster spreads by rhizomes and self-seeds readily once established in open prairie or meadow plantings.

directions: Direct sow into average, well-drained soil in full sun; heath aster is a bushy, fine-textured native prairie perennial with tiny, needle-like leaves that give the whole plant a soft, heath-like appearance well before it blooms. In fall it becomes covered in a dense cloud of small, white, yellow-centered daisy flowers so numerous they can hide the foliage entirely, providing one of the last strong nectar sources for migrating monarchs and other late-season pollinators before frost. It spreads steadily by rhizomes and self-sows in open ground, naturalizing readily in a prairie planting, meadow, or informal border where its late-season froth of white blends well with goldenrods and other fall-blooming natives. Cut back in late fall or winter after bloom and seed drop, and divide congested patches every few years if spread needs to be controlled.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; showy fleabane is native to montane meadows and aspen groves of the Rocky Mountains and adapts well to average garden conditions at lower elevations.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; showy fleabane forms a tidy clump of narrow leaves topped in early to midsummer by abundant lavender-blue, daisy-like flowers with dozens of narrow petals surrounding a bright yellow center, giving the blooms a fine, almost fringed texture reminiscent of a small aster. It is native to montane meadows and aspen groves of the Rocky Mountains, where it blooms heavily for several weeks and attracts a wide range of native bees and butterflies. Unlike many fleabanes, it holds its color and form well without flopping, making it useful as a front-of-border perennial or in naturalistic pollinator plantings at lower elevations outside its mountain habitat. Deadhead spent flowers to prolong bloom, and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Tatarian aster is an unusually tall, sturdy East Asian aster that rarely needs staking despite its height.

directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Tatarian aster is a robust, back-of-border East Asian perennial that towers over most other garden asters, sending up sturdy, largely self-supporting stems topped with broad, flat-topped clusters of lavender-blue, yellow-centered daisy flowers in mid to late fall, among the latest of any hardy aster to bloom. Large, coarse basal leaves form a substantial rosette before the flowering stems rise, giving the plant a strong presence even before bloom. Its late timing makes it valuable for extending pollinator forage right up to the first hard frosts, when few other nectar sources remain. Despite its height, it is notably wind- and rain-resistant compared to many tall perennials, though staking or growing among other sturdy neighbors is still helpful in very exposed sites; divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall so winter cold breaks dormancy naturally, into humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees; all parts of this plant are toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas where children or pets graze on plants.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees; dwarf larkspur is a true spring ephemeral woodland wildflower that emerges, blooms, sets seed, and goes fully dormant within about two months each spring, disappearing completely by early summer well before the tree canopy closes. Deeply cut, delicate foliage sends up short spikes of vivid blue to violet-blue (occasionally white) spurred flowers in early to mid spring, blooming alongside other woodland ephemerals like trillium and bloodroot in undisturbed forest understory. Because the plant vanishes completely by summer, mark its location to avoid accidentally disturbing the dormant roots, and interplant with later-emerging ferns or hostas that fill the same space once the larkspur has gone dormant. All parts are toxic if eaten, a trait shared with cultivated larkspurs and delphiniums, so avoid planting where livestock, pets, or small children might be tempted to sample the foliage.

planting.note: Nick or lightly scarify hard seed coats and sow in fall into loose, well-drained, sandy, low-fertility soil in full sun; sandyland bluebonnet was the original 1901 Texas state flower selection, later broadened to include several related Lupinus species.

directions: Scarify seed lightly and direct sow in fall into loose, sandy, well-drained, lean soil in full sun, since seedlings overwinter as small rosettes and bloom the following spring. Sandyland bluebonnet is shorter and more compact than the better-known Texas bluebonnet (Lupinus texensis), with slightly narrower, more silvery leaflets and a preference for deep, sandy soils over the heavier clays that texensis tolerates. Dense spikes of blue flowers with a white to pale yellow banner spot open in early spring, coinciding with roadside bluebonnet displays throughout its native sandy-soil range in South and East Texas. Do not fertilize or amend the planting site, since this nitrogen-fixing legume performs best in the same lean, low-fertility sand it evolved in, and rich soil produces excess foliage at the expense of bloom. Allow seed pods to fully dry and split on the plant before removing spent growth, since the developing pods reseed the planting for future years.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring into lean, well-drained, dry, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; scarlet beeblossom is a tough, deep-taprooted Great Plains and Southwest native adapted to hot, dry, low-fertility ground.

directions: Direct sow into lean, well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; scarlet beeblossom is a low, wiry-stemmed native perennial with small, narrow leaves and slender spikes of small four-petaled flowers that open white to pale pink in the morning and deepen to a rich rose-red by afternoon, giving each flower spike a two-toned, ombre appearance over the course of a single day. It blooms over a very long season from spring through fall, drawing in hawk moths at dusk along with bees and butterflies during the day, and its deep taproot makes it exceptionally drought tolerant once established while also making mature plants difficult to transplant successfully. It thrives in the same tough, dry, low-fertility soils that support native shortgrass prairie and is an excellent low-water filler for xeriscape beds, rock gardens, and naturalistic plantings. Avoid rich soil and frequent irrigation, which shorten its lifespan and produce lank, floppy growth.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall, 2–3 inches deep, into well-drained, average, prairie-type soil in full sun to partial shade; prairie celestial goes fully dormant in summer heat, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the resting corm.

directions: Plant corms 2 to 3 inches deep in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; prairie celestial is a small, exquisite native bulb of tallgrass and mixed-grass prairies, sending up a few grass-like, pleated leaves in late winter followed by delicate, sky-blue to violet-blue, three-petaled flowers in mid-spring. Individual flowers open only for a single morning and close by early afternoon, especially on sunny days, so the best display is seen on a walk through the planting before midday during the brief two- to three-week bloom window. After flowering and setting seed, the foliage yellows and the plant disappears entirely underground for the rest of the year, re-emerging reliably the following late winter. Because the corm is completely dormant and invisible for most of the year, mark plantings carefully and avoid deep cultivation nearby, and interplant with summer-active prairie grasses or perennials that fill the space once the foliage has died back.

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets (pups) or container-grown plants in spring into very well-drained, gritty, rocky, alkaline soil in full sun; Havard's agave is among the most cold-hardy of all agave species, tolerating temperatures well below 0°F once established.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty, rocky, alkaline soil in full sun; Havard's century plant forms a compact, symmetrical rosette of thick, powdery blue-gray leaves edged with stout, dark reddish-brown teeth and tipped with a sharp terminal spine, native to rocky slopes of the Chihuahuan Desert mountains at elevations that see hard freezes most winters. It is exceptionally cold-hardy for an agave, surviving temperatures well below 0°F in well-drained soil, making it one of the few true agaves reliable outside the mildest desert and coastal climates. Like all agaves, it is monocarpic, growing slowly for many years (often a decade or more) before sending up a tall, branched flower stalk once in its lifetime, after which the main rosette dies, though basal offsets usually continue the clump. Water only to establish young plants, since mature specimens are extremely drought tolerant and prone to rot in wet, poorly drained, or clay-heavy soil.
